common_name: Common Boxwood (American Boxwood, Large-Growing Species Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; common boxwood is the classic large-growing species used for tall hedges, screens, and topiary, distinct from the small, slow-growing 'Suffruticosa' edging form.

directions: Plant in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade appreciated in the hottest parts of zone 8–9; common boxwood is the classic large-growing species behind centuries of formal garden hedging, topiary, and knot gardens, producing dense, small, glossy evergreen leaves on a shrub that, left unclipped, eventually reaches 15–20 feet — considerably larger and faster-growing than the compact 'Suffruticosa' edging boxwood more often used for miniature parterres. Regular shearing two to three times during the growing season maintains a tight, formal hedge or topiary shape; boxwood tolerates hard pruning well and can be shaped into nearly any form. Good air circulation is essential to reduce boxwood blight and leaf spot diseases, both increasingly serious problems in humid climates — avoid overhead watering and dense, unpruned growth that traps moisture. Provide consistent moisture, especially the first two years, and mulch to keep roots cool, since boxwood roots are shallow and sensitive to both drought and waterlogging.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; California privet is one of the most-planted hedge shrubs in North American history, prized for fast, dense growth, though it self-seeds readily and is considered invasive in parts of the country.

directions: Plant in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; California privet is one of the most widely planted formal hedge shrubs in North American landscape history, valued for extremely fast, dense growth, glossy semi-evergreen foliage, and outstanding tolerance of hard, frequent shearing into tight formal hedges, screens, and topiary shapes. Small white flower clusters appear in early summer with a strong fragrance some find pleasant and others find heavy, followed by small blue-black berries that birds spread widely — this vigorous self-seeding has made California privet a documented invasive species in wooded and disturbed areas across much of the eastern and midwestern United States, where it forms dense thickets that crowd out native understory plants. Where hedging is still desired, shear regularly before flowering to reduce berry production and self-seeding, or consider a non-invasive alternative such as Podocarpus, Distylium, or Ternstroemia for new plantings near natural areas. Established hedges tolerate poor soil, pollution, salt spray, and neglect better than almost any other hedging shrub.
sources: invasive species assessments (multiple state extension services)

common_name: Common Privet (European Privet, Classic Deciduous Hedge Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; common privet is the traditional European hedging privet, tolerant of hard shearing and poor soil, though it self-seeds readily and is considered invasive in parts of North America.

directions: Plant in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; common privet is the traditional European hedging shrub behind centuries of formal garden and farmstead hedgerows, valued for tolerating hard, frequent shearing, poor and alkaline soils, and urban pollution better than most flowering shrubs, growing dense and twiggy with small, dark-green, semi-deciduous leaves that persist late into fall. Clusters of small, strongly scented white flowers appear in early summer, followed by small black berries that are mildly toxic if eaten and are spread widely by birds — this readiness to self-seed has made common privet a documented invasive species escaping into woodlands and fencerows across parts of the northeastern and midwestern United States, where it crowds out native shrub-layer plants. Shear two to three times during the growing season to maintain a tight, formal hedge, and consider deadheading or shearing before flowering to reduce berry production and self-seeding where invasive spread near natural areas is a concern.
sources: invasive species assessments (multiple state extension services)

common_name: Glossy Privet (Tree Privet, Evergreen Privet Tree)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; glossy privet grows into a substantial small evergreen tree if left unpruned and self-seeds aggressively — it is a documented invasive species in the Gulf South and should be sheared before flowering or replaced with a non-invasive alternative near natural areas.

directions: Plant in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; glossy privet is a large, fast-growing evergreen shrub or small tree with big, glossy, dark-green leaves and showy panicles of small white flowers in late spring, historically planted as a substantial screening hedge, street tree, or specimen for its handsome, dense evergreen canopy. Left unpruned it grows quickly into a 20–30 foot tree; sheared regularly it can be maintained as a tall, dense hedge or screen. The abundant, heavily fragrant flowers give way to prolific clusters of small blue-black berries that birds spread widely, and glossy privet has become a serious, well-documented invasive species across the Gulf South and much of the southeastern United States, forming dense stands in bottomland forests and disturbed woodland edges that displace native trees and shrubs. Because of this, it is best avoided in new plantings near natural areas — where a large-growing broadleaf evergreen screen is wanted, non-invasive alternatives like Podocarpus macrophyllus, Ilex, or Ternstroemia gymnanthera are strongly preferable.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Invasive Species Guidance

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring on a trellis, fence, or arbor in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; common jasmine is more cold-hardy than tropical jasmines like Arabian or pink jasmine, tolerating brief freezes once established.

directions: Plant on a trellis, fence, arbor, or other sturdy support in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; common jasmine, also called poet's jasmine, is the classic hardy climbing jasmine species long grown for its intensely sweet-scented white, star-shaped flowers, produced in flushes from late spring through summer above delicate, deep-green pinnate foliage. It is the species most associated with the essential oil used in perfumery and is more cold-tolerant than the tropical jasmines popular in warm climates, tolerating brief dips into the low 20s°F once established, though it dies back in a hard freeze and resprouts from the base. The twining stems climb readily onto any support and can also be trained as a loose, informal groundcover or espalier if left untrellised. Prune immediately after the main spring-summer flush to shape the vine and control size, since it blooms on the current season's new growth. Consistent moisture and a sunny to lightly shaded spot with good air circulation encourage the heaviest, most fragrant bloom.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded while the vine climbs into sun; Anemone clematis is an exceptionally vigorous, large climber and needs a sturdy, spacious support such as a large arbor, pergola, or fence.

directions: Plant with roots shaded and cool while the vine climbs into full sun to partial shade on a large, sturdy support; Anemone clematis is one of the most vigorous of all clematis species, capable of quickly covering an arbor, pergola, or fence with a dense curtain of growth and, in mid to late spring, an overwhelming flush of four-petaled, anemone-like flowers in white or soft pink, often fragrant, produced in such profusion that the entire vine can appear smothered in bloom for several weeks. It flowers on the previous year's growth, so it belongs to the group of clematis that should be pruned, if needed, immediately after flowering rather than in late winter — pruning in winter removes the wood that would have flowered that spring. Because of its size and vigor, give it ample space and a support strong enough to bear its eventual weight; it is not well suited to small trellises or delicate structures. Once established it is a tough, long-lived, relatively low-maintenance vine, though it prefers cooler summers and can struggle with the most intense Gulf Coast heat and humidity.
